set: These are the last three of the seven parables of the Kingdom in Matthew 13, spoken to the disciples in the house (13:36). The treasure and the pearl belong together: both men sell all they have. The net, like the weeds among the wheat, speaks of the end of the age, when the good and the bad will be separated.
str: v. 44: the treasure hidden in a field.
vv. 45–46: the merchant and the one pearl.
vv. 47–50: the dragnet and the separation at the end.
vv. 51–52: “Have you understood all this?” and the scribe trained for the Kingdom.
kw: “In his joy he goes and sells all.” The selling is not a heavy loss; joy makes it light.
The scribe of v. 52 has been made a disciple for the Kingdom. He brings out both the new and the old: the Gospel and the Scriptures of Israel together.
vv: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which someone found and hid; then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.
on finding one pearl of great value, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.
The first man stumbles on the treasure; the merchant searches for it. God is found in both ways.
Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like the master of a household who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.
Many see here a portrait of Matthew himself, and of every good teacher in the Church.
ch: The Catechism quotes these parables: to gain the Kingdom one must give everything (CCC 546). On v. 52 the Council recalls St Augustine's rule: the New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New (Dei Verbum 16).

rite: St John Chrysostom (about 349–407), priest of Antioch and later Archbishop of Constantinople, is one of the greatest preachers of the Church; his name means “golden-mouthed”. Antioch is the mother city of the West Syriac tradition to which the Syro-Malankara Church belongs. In Malayalam he is called Mar Ivanios, a form of the name John. The same name was taken by Archbishop Geevarghese Mar Ivanios, who led the reunion of the Malankara Catholic Church with Rome in 1930.
study: What is the “treasure” for which I would gladly sell everything? Does my life show it?
How do the Old and New Testaments help each other in my reading of Scripture?

lead: On the feast of St Philip the Apostle, Paul describes the apostles as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries, judged by the Lord alone. In the Gospel Philip says, “Lord, show us the Father,” and Jesus answers, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” The steward's whole task is to show Christ, and in Christ the Father.

r.h: Stewards of God's mysteries
set: The Corinthians compared their teachers, Paul, Apollos and Cephas, and took sides (1:12; 3:4–5). Paul ends this section by telling them how to think of their ministers: not as heads of parties, but as servants and stewards who must answer to the Lord.
str: v. 1: servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries.
v. 2: what is required of stewards: trustworthiness.
vv. 3–4: Paul does not even judge himself; the Lord judges.
v. 5: do not judge before the time; the Lord will bring to light what is hidden.
kw: The manager of a household, often himself a slave, who gives out what belongs to the master. The steward distributes what is not his own.
The one quality required. Not brilliance, but faithfulness.
vv: Think of us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries.
Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy.
Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart.
Only God sees the heart. This frees ministers both from pride and from the fear of human opinion.
ch: The Church applies this text above all to bishops and priests, who administer the sacraments, the mysteries of God, and must be found faithful. Every baptized person is also a steward, called to use each gift received “like good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10).

r.h: Whoever has seen me has seen the Father
set: The scene is the Last Supper, in Jesus' farewell discourse (John 13–17). Jesus has just said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (14:6). Thomas asked about the way; now Philip asks to see the Father.

Philip came from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter (1:44). In John he brings Nathanael to Jesus (1:45), is tested by Jesus before the feeding of the five thousand (6:5–7), and brings the Greeks who wish to see Jesus (12:21–22). He is a practical and honest man.
str: v. 7: to know Jesus is to know the Father.
v. 8: Philip's request.
vv. 9–11: whoever has seen me has seen the Father; I am in the Father and the Father in me.
v. 12: believers will do greater works.
vv. 13–14: whatever you ask in my name.
kw: Philip's prayer echoes Moses: “Show me your glory, I pray” (Exodus 33:18). What Moses could not see, the disciples see in the face of Jesus.
To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as one united to him, according to his will, for the glory of the Father.
vv: Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied.
Philip asks for the one thing that would satisfy the human heart. Jesus tells him he has had it all along.
Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
A gentle reproach, by name. Jesus is not a messenger pointing beyond himself; he is the image of the Father.
I will do whatever you ask in my name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ's whole life is a revelation of the Father, and cites this verse (CCC 516). The Fathers used John 14:9–10 to show that the Son is one in being with the Father, as the Council of Nicaea confessed (in substance). Prayer in the name of Jesus is the heart of Christian prayer (CCC 2614, 2664–2666).

rite: St Philip the Apostle is remembered today in the Syro-Malankara calendar; the Latin Church keeps his feast with St James on 3 May. An early tradition, recorded by Eusebius, says that Philip was buried at Hierapolis in Asia Minor. His request is the prayer of every seeker, and Jesus' answer is fulfilled at every Holy Qurbono: in the Son we see the Father.
study: What do I ask God to “show” me before I will be satisfied?
How can I be a faithful steward of what I have received, in my family and parish?

lead: Today the Syro-Malankara Church begins the season of Suboro, the “good news” or Annunciation. The first good news of the New Testament is not given in Nazareth but in the Temple of Jerusalem, to an old priest at the hour of incense. The Evening Gospel (Luke 1:1–17) already opens the scene with Luke's preface and the angel's promise.

The four Old Testament lessons all speak of God at work where human hope has run out. Sarah, too old to bear, is promised Isaac (Genesis 17). Ruth the Moabite binds herself to Naomi and to Naomi's God (Ruth 1). Hannah, barren and mocked, pours out her soul at the sanctuary (1 Samuel 1). Isaiah hears God say to a weak people, “Do not fear, for I am with you” (Isaiah 41). The Catholic Epistle (2 Peter 1:3–11) reminds us that God's promises make us “participants of the divine nature”.

We study three readings closely: Genesis 17:15–22, the Old Testament lesson that stands closest to the Gospel and to the Epistle; Romans 4:13–25, where Paul reads that same story as the school of faith; and Luke 1:5–25, the message to Zechariah. The key words are promise, barrenness and believing.

r.h: A son for Abraham and Sarah
set: Genesis 17 is the chapter of the covenant of circumcision. Abraham is ninety-nine years old (17:1). God changes his name from Abram to Abraham, “father of a multitude” (17:5), and gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant (17:9–14).

Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar, is already thirteen (17:25), and Abraham seems to have settled on him as his heir. Today's verses make the promise sharper than ever before: the son of the promise will come from Sarah herself. Chapter 18 tells the same promise again, heard this time by Sarah at the tent door, where she too laughs (18:12) and the Lord asks, “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” (18:14).
str: vv. 15–16: Sarai becomes Sarah; she will be blessed and will be the mother of nations and kings.
v. 17: Abraham falls on his face and laughs.
v. 18: his plea for Ishmael.
vv. 19–21: God's answer: a son from Sarah, named Isaac, the heir of the everlasting covenant; Ishmael too will be blessed.
v. 22: God goes up from Abraham.

¶ The passage has the shape of an annunciation: God appears, gives a message, meets an objection, names the child and fixes the time. Luke's two annunciations, to Zechariah and to Mary, follow the same pattern.
kw: Both Sarai and Sarah are usually understood as forms of the word for “princess”. The new name marks a new mission: kings will come from her (17:16). In the Bible a new name means a new vocation.
The child's name plays on Abraham's laughter (17:17). Later Sarah says, “God has brought laughter for me” (21:6). The laugh of doubt becomes the laugh of joy.
The covenant does not depend on Abraham's strength or age. God binds himself to it for all generations (17:19).
vv: Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed, and said to himself, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?”
Two gestures together: Abraham bows in worship and laughs in disbelief. God does not reject him. He takes the laugh and turns it into the child's name.
God said, “No, but your wife Sarah shall bear you a son, and you shall name him Isaac.
God's “No” to Abraham's smaller hope is a “Yes” to something greater than he dared to ask. Many unanswered prayers are of this kind.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you; I will bless him and make him fruitful and exceedingly numerous;
The name Ishmael means “God hears” (16:11). Even when God chooses another path, he hears the father's prayer for his son.
ch: The New Testament reads Sarah's motherhood as the fruit of faith (Romans 4:19; Hebrews 11:11). The Catechism names Sarah among the holy women of the Old Covenant whose mission prepared for that of Mary: against all human expectation God chooses those who seemed powerless, to show his faithfulness to his promises (CCC 489). The angel's word to Mary, “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37), is the answer to the question asked at Abraham's tent.

r.h: Abraham hoped against hope
set: In Romans 1–3 Paul shows that all, Jews and Gentiles alike, need God's saving justice, and that it is given as a gift through faith in Christ (3:21–26). Chapter 4 brings Abraham as the proof from Scripture: “he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).
In 4:9–12 Paul has noted that Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, before he was circumcised in Genesis 17. So Abraham is the father both of the circumcised and of the Gentiles who believe.
str: vv. 13–15: the promise did not come through the law.
vv. 16–17: it rests on faith so that it may be grace, for all Abraham's children.
vv. 18–21: a portrait of Abraham's faith before an old body and a barren womb.
v. 22: therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness.
vv. 23–25: the same is written for us who believe in the God who raised Jesus.
kw: The key word of the chapter. A promise depends on the one who makes it. That is why it can rest on grace (v. 16).

A word from accounting, used again and again in this chapter. God enters faith into the account as righteousness. The Church understands this not as a mere label but as a real gift that makes us just (CCC 1992).
Literally “beyond hope, upon hope” (v. 18). Every human reason for hope had gone; Abraham rested on God's word.
vv: in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.
Two titles of God: he raises the dead and he creates from nothing. Abraham's “dead” body, Sarah's barren womb and the tomb of Jesus are three places where this God has acted.
Hoping against hope, he believed that he would become “the father of many nations,”
He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was already as good as dead (for he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb.

A note on the text. Many later manuscripts read “he did not consider his own body”, as in older English Bibles. The oldest manuscripts, followed by the NRSV and the POC, say that he did consider it. Faith here does not close its eyes to the facts; it looks at them squarely and still trusts God.
who was handed over to death for our trespasses and was raised for our justification.
The words “handed over” echo the Greek of the Servant song (Isaiah 53:12). The Resurrection is not only proof of salvation; it belongs to salvation itself.
ch: The Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith and quotes Paul: “hoping against hope” he believed (CCC 145–146). It cites Romans 4:25 to teach that the Paschal mystery has two sides: by his death Christ delivers us from sin, and by his Resurrection he opens the way to new life, which is above all justification (CCC 654). The Council of Trent called faith “the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification” (Session 6, chapter 8). Catholics and Lutherans set out their shared understanding of this teaching in the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999).

r.h: The message to Zechariah in the Temple
set: Luke opens with a careful Greek preface for Theophilus (1:1–4, read at the Evening Gospel), then changes style and tells the story in the language of the Greek Old Testament. “King Herod of Judea” is Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC.

The priests were divided into twenty-four courses (1 Chronicles 24); the course of Abijah was the eighth (24:10). Each course served in the Temple for a week, twice a year. Incense was offered every morning and evening on the golden altar inside the Holy Place, and the priest was chosen by lot. Later Jewish tradition (the Mishnah) says that only priests who had never offered incense took part in that lot, so for Zechariah this was the hour of his life.
In that culture childlessness was felt as a public disgrace (1:25). Luke insists that it was not a punishment: both were “righteous before God” (1:6).
str: vv. 5–7: a righteous, childless, aging couple.
vv. 8–10: the hour of incense; the people pray outside.
vv. 11–17: the angel and the message: a son named John, the forerunner with the spirit of Elijah.
vv. 18–20: Zechariah's question and the sign of silence.
vv. 21–23: the waiting people and the mute priest.
vv. 24–25: Elizabeth conceives.
¶ Luke sets this scene beside the annunciation to Mary (1:26–38): the Temple and a village, an old priest and a young woman, a question of doubt and a question of faith.
kw: “the Lord remembered” / “the Lord has shown favour”
The names tell the story: God remembers, and God gives grace. Elizabeth's name is that of Aaron's wife, Elisheba (Exodus 6:23): this is a wholly priestly family.
The angel who came to Daniel “at the time of the evening sacrifice” (Daniel 9:21) comes again at the hour of incense. The time of fulfilment has arrived.
Luke's first use of the verb of the Gospel (1:19). The Syriac name of the season, Suboro, carries the same meaning: the message, the good news.
vv: But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will name him John.
Which prayer? Perhaps the old prayer for a child, which he may have stopped praying; perhaps the priest's prayer for the redemption of Israel. In John both are answered at once.
With the spirit and power of Elijah he will go before him, to turn the hearts of parents to their children,
The angel quotes Malachi 4:5–6, the last words of the prophets in our Old Testament. “Before him” means before the Lord God (v. 16). As the Gospel unfolds, the Lord whom John precedes is Jesus.
But now, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time, you will become mute, unable to speak, until the day these things occur.

The silence is both discipline and sign. When the child is named, Zechariah's mouth is opened and his first words are praise (1:64). The priest who could not bless the waiting people (v. 22) foreshadows the end of the Gospel, where Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his disciples, who return to the Temple praising God (24:50–53).
ch: The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate precursor, sent to prepare his way, “more than a prophet” (CCC 523), and teaches that in him the Holy Spirit completes the preparation of the people for the Lord; he was filled with the Spirit even from his mother's womb (CCC 717–718). St Ambrose, commenting on Luke, praises Zechariah and Elizabeth as righteous in both priestly and married life (in substance). St Ephrem contrasts the priest who doubted and was made silent with the Virgin who believed and conceived the Word (in substance).

qa: Mary also asked “How?”. Why was only Zechariah made silent?

Zechariah asked for proof: “How will I know that this is so?” (1:18). Mary asked how it would happen, since she had no husband, and then gave her full consent (1:34, 38). Elizabeth's words sum up the difference: “blessed is she who believed” (1:45).
Did Abraham lack faith when he laughed?

His laugh mixed wonder and doubt, but Paul can still say he “did not weaken in faith” (Romans 4:19), because Abraham obeyed and held on to the promise. Faith is not the absence of every question; it is trust that keeps walking with God.
Does Romans 4 mean good works do not matter?

No. Paul says that justification cannot be earned; it is God's gift received in faith. The same Paul says that what counts is “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Good works are the fruit of grace, not the price of it.
rite: Suboro opens the Malankara cycle of the Annunciation Sundays: the message to Zechariah, the message to Mary, the Visitation, the birth of John the Baptist, the revelation to Joseph, and the Sunday before Christmas. In the West Syriac tradition incense accompanies the great prayers of the priest, such as the Sedro, while the people stand and pray, just as the people prayed outside at the hour of incense in Luke. At every Holy Qurbono we stand where Zechariah stood, but we receive more than a promise: the One whom John announced comes to the altar in his Body and Blood.
study: God's “No” to Abraham's prayer for Ishmael hid a greater “Yes”. Where have I seen this in my own life?
Paul says Abraham looked squarely at his “dead” body and still believed. What fact in my life do I need to face with faith rather than avoid?
Zechariah may have stopped praying for a child. Which prayers have I given up on?
How can our family or parish keep Suboro as a season of listening, like Zechariah in his silence?

lead: Today the Syro-Malankara Church remembers Mar Mathai Shleeha, St Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist. The Gospel tells his call at the tax booth; the Epistle shows what every call leads to: a life worthy of it, lived in the unity of one body. The tax collector who got up and followed becomes a member, and a builder, of the one family of God.

r.h: Lead a life worthy of your calling
set: Ephesians falls into two halves. Chapters 1–3 praise God's plan to unite all things in Christ and to make Jews and Gentiles one body. Chapters 4–6 draw the practical consequences, and the first word, “therefore”, links the two. Paul writes as “the prisoner in the Lord” (see 3:1; 6:20).
str: v. 1: the appeal: live worthy of your calling.
vv. 2–3: the virtues that keep unity: humility, gentleness, patience, love, peace.
vv. 4–6: seven “ones”, rising to the one God and Father of all.
kw: The same root as “church” (ekklēsia, the assembly of those called). A Christian life is an answer to someone who called first.
In Greek culture lowliness was mostly the attitude of a slave. Christians, following the humble Christ (Philippians 2:8), made it the first virtue of life together.
vv: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to lead a life worthy of the calling to which you have been called,
A prisoner begs. Paul does not command from a position of power; his chains give weight to his plea.
making every effort to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Unity is the Spirit's gift; we do not create it, but we must work hard to keep it.
one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
ch: The Catechism sums up the unity of the Church in these verses: she acknowledges one Lord, confesses one faith, is born of one Baptism, forms one Body, is given life by one Spirit, for the sake of one hope (CCC 866). The Second Vatican Council's decree on ecumenism quotes “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” as the foundation of the search for unity among Christians (Unitatis Redintegratio 2).

r.h: The call of Matthew
set: Mark and Luke tell this call of a tax collector named Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27). The First Gospel names him Matthew, and in the list of the Twelve calls him “Matthew the tax collector” (10:3). The scene is Capernaum, on a trade road near the border, where tolls were charged on goods. Toll collectors worked for the ruling power, often overcharged, and were counted with sinners.
str: v. 9: the call and the immediate answer.
v. 10: a meal with tax collectors and sinners.
v. 11: the Pharisees' objection.
vv. 12–13: Jesus' answer in three steps: a proverb, a text of Scripture, a statement of his mission.
kw: Not a high official but the man at the booth. Matthew's profession was a byword for greed.
Hosea 6:6 has the Hebrew ḥesed, steadfast covenant love. Only Matthew among the Gospels quotes this verse, and he quotes it twice (9:13; 12:7).
vv: he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth; and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
Two words of Jesus, and no words from Matthew: only action. “Got up” is the same verb used for rising from the dead.
“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.
Go and learn what this means, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I have come to call not the righteous but sinners.”
“Go and learn” is a rabbi's formula for sending students back to study a text. Hosea does not reject worship; he says that worship without mercy does not please God.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse to show that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom (CCC 545). St Bede, preaching on this Gospel, said that Jesus looked at Matthew “by having mercy and by choosing” (miserando atque eligendo), the words Pope Francis took as his episcopal motto.

qa: Are Matthew and Levi the same person?
The Church has generally understood so: the three Gospels tell the same scene, and Matthew alone gives the apostle's name. Like Simon Peter, a person could carry two names.
rite: The Malankara calendar keeps St Matthew on 16 November. Early tradition, recorded by Papias and Eusebius, says Matthew first gathered the sayings of the Lord in the Hebrew language; the traditions about the place of his preaching and martyrdom differ. In the Holy Qurbono the Gospel is read with lights and incense: we honour Matthew best by listening to the Gospel that bears his name.
study: Matthew answered with action, not words. What step of following have I been postponing?
Paul names humility, gentleness and patience as the guardians of unity. Which of these does my family most need this week?

lead: Both readings speak of belonging by grace. Paul warns Gentile believers, grafted into Israel's olive tree, not to boast: they stand only by faith. In the Gospel, a paralysed man carried by his friends receives first the forgiveness of his sins and then the use of his legs. In both, what we have is received, not earned.

r.h: Grafted into the olive tree
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's anguished reflection on his own people, most of whom had not accepted Jesus as Messiah. He insists that God has not rejected his people (11:1), and that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). The olive tree is an old image for Israel (Jeremiah 11:16).
str: vv. 17–18: you, the wild shoot, share the rich root: do not boast.
vv. 19–21: they were broken off through unbelief; you stand through faith: stand in awe.
v. 22: the kindness and the severity of God.
vv. 23–24: God can graft the natural branches back in.
kw: The root is the patriarchs and God's promises to them (11:16, 28). The Church lives from Israel's root, not the other way round.
Farmers grafted cultivated shoots onto wild stock. Paul knows he is describing the opposite, and says so: it is “contrary to nature” (v. 24). Grace does what nature cannot.
vv: do not boast over the branches. If you do boast, remember that it is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you.
They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand only through faith. So do not become proud, but stand in awe.
The warning is for Christians. Pride over others is the surest way to lose what we have received.
how much more will these natural branches be grafted back into their own olive tree.
Paul's hope for Israel is not weaker than his warning; it is stronger.
ch: The Second Vatican Council takes up this image: the Church draws sustenance from the root of that good olive tree onto which the wild shoots, the Gentiles, have been grafted (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism teaches the Church's unique bond with the Jewish people, to whom God's call is irrevocable (CCC 839).

r.h: The paralytic forgiven and healed
set: “His own town” is Capernaum, where Jesus made his home (4:13). Mark tells the same story with the roof opened above Jesus (Mark 2:1–12); Matthew tells it more briefly, so that the question of authority stands out.
str: vv. 1–2: the man is carried in; Jesus sees their faith and forgives.
v. 3: the scribes think “blasphemy”.
vv. 4–6: Jesus' question and the sign.
vv. 7–8: the man goes home; the crowds glorify God.
kw: Jesus' first word is courage, then forgiveness. The same word is spoken to the woman with the haemorrhage (9:22).
Not raw power but rightful authority. To forgive sins belongs to God alone; Jesus claims it as the Son of Man.
vv: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven.”
“Their faith”: the friends' faith counts. This does not mean the illness was caused by a personal sin (see John 9:3); Jesus goes first to the deepest need.
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
Forgiveness cannot be seen; healing can. The visible sign confirms the invisible gift.
When the crowds saw it, they were filled with awe, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.
“To human beings”, in the plural. Matthew's readers would think of the authority given to the Church to bind and loose (16:19; 18:18).
ch: The Catechism teaches that only God forgives sins, that Jesus, as Son of God, says of himself that he has this authority on earth, and that he gave this power to men to exercise in his name (CCC 1441–1442). This is what happens in the sacrament of Confession.

qa: Was the man paralysed because he had sinned?
The Gospel does not say so. Jesus elsewhere rejects that simple link (John 9:3). He forgives first because sin is the deeper paralysis of every human being.
study: Paul says, “it is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you.” What do I owe to those who handed on the faith to me?
Whom could I “carry” to Jesus this week, by prayer or by bringing them to Confession?

lead: Two farewells. Paul, near the end of his life, closes his last letter with names of friends and a blessing. Jesus, near the end of his ministry, weeps over Jerusalem with the image of a hen gathering her chicks. Both show love that keeps reaching out, even to the end.

r.h: The Lord be with your spirit
set: 2 Timothy presents itself as Paul's last letter, written from prison in Rome as he awaits death: “I am already being poured out as a libation” (4:6). Many companions have left him; only Luke is with him (4:11). The letter ends with greetings.
str: v. 19: greetings to friends in Ephesus.
v. 20: news of two co-workers.
v. 21: “come before winter”; greetings from Rome.
v. 22: the closing blessing.
kw: A blessing on the whole person. The liturgy's dialogue, “The Lord be with you. And with your spirit”, grows from greetings like this (see also Galatians 6:18; Philemon 25).
Sea travel stopped in the winter months. If Timothy delayed, he might not reach Paul in time.
vv: Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus.
Prisca and Aquila, the tentmaker couple, worked with Paul in Corinth and Ephesus (Acts 18). Onesiphorus was not ashamed of Paul's chains and searched for him in Rome (1:16–17).
Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus sends greetings to you, as do Pudens and Linus and Claudia and all the brothers and sisters.
St Irenaeus records that the apostles entrusted the Church of Rome to Linus, the first successor of Peter. Here he is simply one of the brothers sending greetings.
The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
“Your” is singular, for Timothy; “you” in the last line is plural. The letter was meant to be read to the whole Church.
ch: The great teaching of Paul ends with names. The Church remembers that holiness is lived with people, in friendship and loyalty. Every time the priest greets us and we answer, “And with your spirit”, we pray the same blessing that Paul sent to Timothy.

r.h: As a hen gathers her brood
set: These verses close Jesus' long rebuke of the scribes and Pharisees in the Temple (Matthew 23). Right after it, he leaves the Temple (24:1). The rebuke ends not in anger but in a lament, like the laments of the prophets over Jerusalem.
str: v. 37: the lament and the image of the hen.
v. 38: “your house is left to you, desolate.”
v. 39: “until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes…’”
kw: The same verb is used for the gathering of the elect at the coming of the Son of Man (24:31). Jesus' wish is to gather, never to scatter.
Here the Temple, the house of God, which becomes “your house” when God's presence is refused (compare Jeremiah 22:5).
vv: How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
A mother's image for God, as in the Psalms: “under his wings you will find refuge”. The divine longing meets the human power to refuse.
See, your house is left to you, desolate.
For I tell you, you will not see me again until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’
Psalm 118:26, the words the crowds sang when Jesus entered the city (21:9). The lament ends with a door left open.
ch: This is a lament of love, not a curse on a people. The Church teaches that the guilt of Christ's death cannot be laid on all the Jews then living, nor on the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). St Anselm, in his prayer to St Paul, takes up this verse and calls Jesus a mother who gathers her chicks under her wings (in substance).

study: Paul's last words are names of friends. Whom would I name, and have I thanked them?
Where in my life does Christ want to gather me “under his wings”, and where am I unwilling?

lead: Both readings are about authority as service. Paul tells children to honour their parents and tells fathers not to crush their children. Jesus warns against leaders who load burdens on others and love titles: among his disciples, the greatest is the servant.

r.h: Children and parents in the Lord
set: These verses belong to the “household code” of Ephesians (5:21–6:9), which addresses wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. The whole code is governed by its first line: “Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:21). Children are addressed directly: they were present when the letter was read in the assembly.
str: vv. 1–3: children: obey and honour, with the promise of the commandment.
v. 4: fathers: do not provoke; bring up in the Lord.
kw: Literally “listen under”: obedience begins with listening.
Formation by example and correction, and formation by word. Both are “of the Lord”: parents form children for Christ, not for themselves.
vv: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
this is the first commandment with a promise:
Exodus 20:12 and Deuteronomy 5:16. The commandment to honour parents is the first that carries a promise of blessing.
And, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
Roman law gave the father almost unlimited power over his children. Paul sets a limit to that power in the name of Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that children owe their parents respect, gratitude and, while they live at home, obedience (CCC 2214–2217), and that parents are the first ones responsible for the education of their children (CCC 2223). St John Paul II called the family's right and duty to educate “essential” and “irreplaceable” (Familiaris Consortio 36).

r.h: The greatest among you will be your servant
set: Matthew 23 opens Jesus' last public discourse in the Temple. Matthew wrote for a Church living in tension with the synagogue leaders of his time, and that tension shows. Yet Jesus' words are not aimed at a people. They warn every religious leader, the Church's own shepherds first of all, against saying without doing.
str: vv. 1–3: do what they teach, not what they do.
v. 4: heavy burdens on others.
vv. 5–7: religion for display.
vv. 8–10: one Teacher, one Father, one Instructor.
vv. 11–12: the servant is the greatest.
kw: “Moses' seat” means the authority to teach the Law; stone seats of honour have been found in ancient synagogues. Our word “cathedral”, the church of the bishop's chair, comes from the same word.
Small boxes with Scripture verses worn for prayer (Deuteronomy 6:8) and tassels on the cloak (Numbers 15:38–39). Jesus himself wore the fringe (9:20). He criticises not the custom but the display.
The word from which “deacon” comes. Authority in the Church is measured by service.
vv: therefore, do whatever they teach you and follow it; but do not do as they do, for they do not practice what they teach.
Jesus respects the teaching office even when its holders fail. The word of God keeps its value even on unworthy lips.
And call no one your father on earth, for you have one Father
The greatest among you will be your servant. All who exalt themselves will be humbled, and all who humble themselves will be exalted.
The whole passage is summed up here, in Jesus' own life: he came “not to be served but to serve” (20:28).
ch: The Catechism teaches that ministry in the Church is by its nature service: those who receive it become servants of Christ (CCC 876). St Gregory the Great chose for the pope the title “servant of the servants of God”.

qa: If Jesus says “call no one father”, why do we call priests “Father”?

Jesus forbids putting any human being in the place of God, the source of all fatherhood. He does not forbid the word: Paul writes, “in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). A priest is called father because he serves the fatherhood of God, not because he replaces it.
study: Ephesians 6:4 says “do not provoke your children to anger.” What in my words or habits provokes anger at home?
Where am I tempted to “say and not do”?

lead: Today's readings are about the word that comes near. Paul says the word of faith is already on our lips and in our hearts. Jesus tells of a sower who throws that word everywhere, and of the different soils that receive it. The seed is the same; the soil makes the difference.

r.h: The word is near you
set: In Romans 9–11 Paul asks why many in Israel have not believed in Christ. In chapter 10 he contrasts two ways: righteousness sought through the Law and righteousness received through faith. He uses Moses' own words in Deuteronomy 30:12–14, where God says his commandment is not far away, and reads them in the light of Christ.
str: v. 5: the way of the Law (Leviticus 18:5).
vv. 6–8: faith speaks: no need to climb to heaven or descend to the abyss; the word is near.
vv. 9–10: confess with the lips, believe in the heart.
vv. 11–13: everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved, Jew and Greek alike.
kw: The spoken word, the message proclaimed. Faith comes from hearing it (10:17).
Literally “to say the same thing”: to say with the Church what God has said.
The Greek Old Testament uses this word for the divine name. In v. 13 Paul quotes Joel's “the Lord” and applies it to Jesus.
vv: “The word is near you, on your lips and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
Christ does not have to be fetched from heaven or from the dead; he has come down and has risen. He comes near in the word preached.
because if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
“Jesus is Lord” is one of the oldest Christian creeds. Lips and heart belong together: inner faith and public confession.
For, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.”
Joel 2:32. The word “everyone” is repeated: no one is excluded.
ch: The Catechism explains that by giving Jesus the divine title “Lord”, the first confessions of faith declared that the honour and glory due to God the Father are due also to Jesus (CCC 446–451). From the beginning the Church expressed her faith in short formulas such as this (CCC 186).

r.h: The parable of the sower
set: Matthew 13 is the third of the five great discourses of Jesus in Matthew, the discourse in parables. Jesus sits in a boat, using the water as his pulpit, while the crowd stands on the shore. The explanation of this parable comes later (13:18–23).
str: vv. 1–3a: the scene by the sea.
vv. 3b–8: the sower and four kinds of ground: path, rock, thorns, good soil.
v. 9: “Let anyone with ears listen!”
kw: Greek for the Hebrew māšāl, a comparison or a riddle. A parable draws the hearer in and asks for a response.
An unusually rich harvest, a sign of God's blessing, like Isaac's harvest (Genesis 26:12).
vv: And he told them many things in parables, saying: “Listen! A sower went out to sow.
The sower seems careless: he sows on the path and the rock too. God's word is offered to everyone, without calculation.
Other seeds fell on good soil and brought forth grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
Three quarters of the seed seem lost, but the harvest outweighs all the losses. The parable is an encouragement to sowers.
Let anyone with ears listen!
An echo of the great prayer of Israel, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4). The parable puts the question to the hearer: what kind of soil am I?
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' invitation to the Kingdom comes in the form of parables, and that the parables are like mirrors: will the hearer be hard soil or good earth (CCC 546)? Our response to the word decides what fruit it bears.

study: Paul joins lips and heart. Is my faith stronger inside or in what I say before others?
Which of the four soils best describes my heart this week, and what would make it good soil?

lead: Today the Church celebrates the Entry of Mary, Mother of God, into the Temple. The story of the child Mary brought by Joachim and Anne to the Temple and given to God is not in the Bible; it comes from early Christian tradition, especially the second-century Protoevangelium of James. The feast was kept in the East from the sixth century, linked with the dedication of the New Church of St Mary in Jerusalem (543), and the West received it later. What it celebrates is biblical: Mary belonged wholly to God from the beginning.

The readings do not tell the story of the feast; they show its meaning. Paul's call to rejoice, to pray without anxiety and to think on what is true and pure describes the heart of one given to God. In the Gospel Jesus names as his mother and brothers “whoever does the will of my Father in heaven”, and no one did that will more fully than Mary. The key words are joy, peace and the Father's will.

r.h: Rejoice in the Lord always
set: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison (1:7, 13), not knowing whether he will live or die (1:20–24). Yet joy runs through the whole letter. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first city in Europe where Paul founded a church, beginning with Lydia and her household (Acts 16).
Just before today's verses Paul begs two women, Euodia and Syntyche, “to be of the same mind in the Lord” (4:2). His call to joy and peace is addressed to a real community with real quarrels.
str: v. 4: rejoice, and again rejoice.
v. 5: let your gentleness be known; the Lord is near.
vv. 6–7: no anxiety, but prayer with thanksgiving; God's peace will guard you.
v. 8: think about whatever is true, honourable, just, pure.
v. 9: do what you have learned from me; the God of peace will be with you.
kw: Also an everyday greeting. The angel greets Mary with the same word, chaire (Luke 1:28). Christian joy is not a mood; it is “in the Lord”, so it can exist even in prison.
Reasonableness, a yielding spirit that does not insist on its rights. Paul wants it “known to everyone”.
A military word: a garrison keeping a city. Philippi knew Roman soldiers well. God's peace stands guard over heart and mind.
The same verb Paul uses for God “reckoning” faith as righteousness. Here: take these things into account, let them fill your mind.
vv: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, Rejoice.
A prisoner commands joy. The repetition shows that he means it.
Do not worry about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.
Prayer is the cure for anxiety, and thanksgiving is its key. Every need can become a petition.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
Not the peace of having no problems, but God's own peace, standing guard in the middle of them.

Finally, beloved, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is pleasing, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.
Paul borrows words that the best Greek moralists also prized. Whatever is truly good, wherever it is found, belongs to Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that every need can become the object of prayer of petition, and that thanksgiving belongs to every prayer, as Paul says (CCC 2629–2633; 2637–2638). The Church applies Paul's words to Mary on her feasts: the one who said “my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour” (Luke 1:47) is the model of joy in the Lord and of a mind set on what is pure and true.

r.h: Whoever does the will of my Father
set: This scene ends Matthew 12, a chapter of conflict: disputes over the Sabbath, the charge that Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul, and the demand for a sign. Right after it, Jesus goes out of the house and teaches in parables (13:1). Mark's version adds that his family had come because people said he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21); Matthew does not include that.
str: v. 46: his mother and brothers stand outside.
v. 47: someone tells him.
v. 48: “Who is my mother?”
v. 49: he points to his disciples.
v. 50: the saying about the Father's will.
kw: The family stands outside, the disciples sit around him. Matthew is not judging Mary but showing the new family, gathered around Jesus and his word.
The same will of the Lord's Prayer, “Your will be done” (6:10), and of Gethsemane (26:42). The new family is formed by doing it.
In Hebrew and Aramaic the word for brother also covers cousins and relatives (Genesis 13:8 calls Abraham and his nephew Lot “kindred”, literally brothers).
vv: But to the one who had told him this, Jesus replied, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?”

A note on the text. Verse 47 is missing in some important early manuscripts (the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Vaticanus). The NRSV and the POC print it; the meaning of the scene is the same either way.
And pointing to his disciples, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers!
The gesture matters as much as the words: Jesus stretches out his hand over his disciples.
For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”
This is not a rejection of Mary. It names what made her mother in the deepest sense. She said, “let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).
ch: St Augustine taught that Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (in substance, On Holy Virginity 3). The Second Vatican Council says that during her Son's preaching Mary received his words praising those who hear the word of God and keep it, as she herself was faithfully doing (Lumen Gentium 58). The Catechism calls her the most perfect embodiment of the obedience of faith (CCC 148).

qa: Is the story of Mary's presentation in the Temple in the Bible?

No. It comes from the Protoevangelium of James, a second-century writing that the Church did not receive into the Bible. The feast does not ask us to accept its details. It celebrates a truth of faith: Mary, preserved from sin, belonged wholly to God from the start of her life.
Did Jesus push his mother away?

No. Jesus lifts the conversation from family by blood to family by faith, and Mary belongs to both. Luke's version ends with “those who hear the word of God and do it” (Luke 8:21), which is exactly what Luke says of Mary (1:38, 45; 2:19).
Did Jesus have brothers and sisters?

The Church teaches that Mary remained a virgin. The “brothers” of Jesus are relatives: James and Joseph, named among them (Matthew 13:55), are sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56). The Catechism explains this in CCC 499–501.
rite: The Syro-Malankara Church, with the other Churches of the East, keeps this feast on 21 November, and in her prayers calls Mary Yoldath Aloho, Mother of God. The feast has a quiet link with last Sunday's reading of Hannah: as Hannah gave Samuel to the Lord at the sanctuary, tradition tells that Joachim and Anne gave Mary. The child given to the Temple would become the true Temple, carrying God's Son. It is a fitting day for parents to give their children to God again, and for all of us to renew the gift of ourselves at the Holy Qurbono.
study: Paul commands joy from prison. What would “rejoice in the Lord” mean in my present difficulty?
Philippians 4:6 joins prayer and thanksgiving. For what can I thank God before I ask him for anything today?
Jesus says his true family are those who do the Father's will. What is the Father's will for me this week, in one concrete thing?
Mary was given to God as a child. What did my parents give to God when they brought me to baptism, and how can I renew it?

lead: On the Sunday of the Annunciation to Mary, Mother of God, the West Syriac Church stands at the second step of the Suboro season, the Sundays of announcement that lead to Yeldo, the Nativity. The readings trace one long promise. In the evening Gospel Matthew opens his book with the genealogy (Matthew 1:1–17): forty-two generations of a family through which God kept his word. The Old Testament lessons announce a birth that only God can give: the first promise to the woman in Eden (Genesis 3:8–15), the angel who announces Samson to a barren woman (Judges 13:2–14), the temple rebuilt “not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” (Zechariah 4:6), and Isaiah's cry, “O that you would tear open the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). The Catholic Epistle tells us what that coming makes of us: “See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God” (1 John 3:1).

The three readings studied here form a single line. Genesis gives the promise: the offspring of the woman will strike the serpent's head. Galatians names the moment: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman”. Luke shows the woman herself, in Nazareth, saying yes. Promise, fullness, consent: the key words of this Sunday.

r.h: Where are you? The first promise
set: The scene comes straight after the sin of Genesis 3:1–7. The man and the woman have eaten from the forbidden tree, their eyes are opened, and they sew fig leaves together. Now God comes into the garden, and what follows has the shape of a trial: the Judge questions, the accused answer, and sentence is given.

Genesis 1–11 is not a history book in the modern sense. It teaches, in images, real truths about God, the world and man, among them a real fall at the beginning of human history (CCC 390). The garden, the tree and the serpent carry that teaching.
str: v. 8: the sound of God walking in the garden; the man and woman hide.
vv. 9–10: the first question, “Where are you?”, and the first confession of fear.
vv. 11–13: two more questions; the man blames the woman (and God who gave her), the woman blames the serpent.
vv. 14–15: the sentence on the serpent, which ends in a promise.
¶ God questions the man and the woman, but he does not curse them. He curses only the serpent here (v. 14) and the ground later (v. 17). In the middle of judgment a door to hope is already open.
kw: One Hebrew word. God is not asking for information. It is the call of a father to a child who is hiding, and it is the first question God asks in the Bible. All of salvation history is God looking for man.
A lasting hostility, not a passing quarrel. God himself puts it there: “I will put enmity”. The woman and her offspring will not be on the serpent's side.
The word can mean a whole line of descendants or one single descendant. The verse begins with the line (“your offspring and hers”) and ends with one person: “he will strike your head”.
The same verb is used for both blows: he strikes the head, the serpent strikes the heel. The struggle is real on both sides, but a wound on the heel is not the same as a blow to the head.
vv: But the Lord God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
The man ran from God; God comes after the man. The hiding began with fear (v. 10), and fear is still what keeps people away from God's call.
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.”

Sin has already broken the unity of the couple. A few verses earlier he called her “bone of my bones” (2:23); now she is “the woman whom you gave”. The blame passes on to the woman, and through her even to God.
I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.

A note on the text. The Hebrew has “he” (hû’), and the Greek Septuagint uses a masculine pronoun (autos), pointing to one person, the Messiah. Many Latin manuscripts of the Vulgate read ipsa, “she will crush”, and older Catholic art shows Mary with her foot on the serpent. Both readings carry the same faith: the victory is Christ's, and his mother shares in it as the new Eve.
ch: The Catechism calls Genesis 3:15 the Protoevangelium, the “first gospel”: the first announcement of the Messiah and Redeemer, of a battle between the serpent and the woman, and of the final victory of her descendant. Many Fathers and Doctors of the Church have seen the woman as Mary, the mother of Christ, the “new Eve” (CCC 410–411).

St Justin Martyr and St Irenaeus set Eve and Mary side by side. St Irenaeus writes that the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by Mary's obedience; what the virgin Eve bound through unbelief, the Virgin Mary loosed through faith (CCC 494; Lumen Gentium 56).

r.h: God sent his Son, born of a woman
set: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, in the centre of Asia Minor, which he had founded. After he left, other teachers told the Gentile believers that they must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to belong fully to God's people. In chapters 3–4 Paul answers: we are children of Abraham and heirs of God through faith in Christ, not through the works of the Law.

This passage is the only place where Paul speaks, even indirectly, of the mother of Jesus. It is also one of the earliest Christian texts about the Incarnation, written within about twenty-five years of the Resurrection.
str: vv. 1–2: a picture from family law: an heir who is still a child lives under guardians until the date set by his father.
v. 3: the application: “so with us”; before Christ we were like minors, enslaved to “the elemental spirits of the world”.
vv. 4–5: the first sending: God sends his Son, to redeem and to make us children.
vv. 6–7: the second sending: God sends the Spirit of his Son into our hearts; so we are no longer slaves but children and heirs.

¶ The passage is built on two sendings with the same verb: God sent his Son (v. 4), God sent the Spirit of his Son (v. 6). The Father sends, the Son redeems, the Spirit cries out in us. It is a short lesson on the Holy Trinity.
kw: Time is pictured as a vessel being filled. The coming of the Son is not an accident of history but the moment the Father had fixed (compare v. 2, “the date set by the father”).
Paul says nothing of a human father. The phrase stresses that the Son of God became truly human, with a real mother, in a real family, “under the law”.
A legal word: to be placed as a son, with full rights of inheritance. We are not children of God by nature, as the Son is, but by grace we receive the same name and the same inheritance.

An Aramaic word, the way a son or daughter spoke to their own father. Jesus prayed with it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). Paul keeps the Aramaic even in a Greek letter: the Spirit lets us pray with the very words of Jesus.
vv: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,

Four short phrases hold the whole mystery of Christmas: the time (fullness), the sender (God), the one sent (his Son), and the way he came (born of a woman, born under the law). He comes in humility, inside the history of Israel.
And because you are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”
Notice who cries out. It is the Spirit, crying in our hearts. When we pray “Our Father”, it is the Spirit of the Son praying in us.
So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if a child then also an heir, through God.
Paul suddenly turns from “we” to “you” in the singular. Each believer is meant to hear it personally: you are no longer a slave.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on Jesus Christ with this text (CCC 422) and says that the Annunciation to Mary inaugurates “the fullness of time” (CCC 484). It also teaches that the One whom the Father sends into our hearts, the Spirit of his Son, is truly God (CCC 689). The verses are a key text of the Church's faith that Christ is true God and true man, and that Mary is truly his mother.

r.h: Here am I, the servant of the Lord
set: Luke opens his Gospel with two announcements set side by side. The first (1:5–25) takes place in the Temple in Jerusalem, to an old priest, Zechariah, who asks for a sign and is struck dumb. The second takes place in Nazareth, a small village in Galilee never mentioned in the Old Testament, to a young girl engaged to Joseph. The angel is the same, Gabriel, whom the book of Daniel already knows as the messenger of the end times (Daniel 9:21).
In Jewish custom, the engagement was a binding marriage contract. The bride normally stayed in her father's house for some months before she was taken into her husband's home.
str: vv. 26–27: the sending: time (the sixth month), place (Nazareth), person (a virgin, of the house of David through Joseph).
vv. 28–29: the greeting and Mary's troubled reflection.
vv. 30–33: the first message: a son named Jesus, who will be the Davidic king forever.
v. 34: Mary's question.
vv. 35–37: the second message: the Holy Spirit, the power of the Most High, the Son of God; and a sign, Elizabeth.
v. 38: Mary's answer, and the angel departs.
kw: The ordinary Greek greeting, but its root meaning is “rejoice”. Zephaniah 3:14 calls on the “daughter Zion” to rejoice because the Lord is in her midst; many commentators hear that call behind the angel's word.
A perfect passive participle: one who has been filled with grace and remains so. The angel uses it in place of her name, as if it were a new name. The Malayalam POC renders it ദൈവകൃപ നിറഞ്ഞവളേ.

The word used in the Greek Old Testament for the cloud that covered the tent of meeting when God's glory filled it (Exodus 40:35), and in Luke for the cloud at the Transfiguration (9:34). Mary becomes the new dwelling place of God.
The feminine of doulos, servant or slave. Mary takes the same title as Moses, David and the prophets, “servant of the Lord”, and gives it its fullest meaning.
vv: And he came to her and said, “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.”
“The Lord is with you” was said to Gideon (Judges 6:12) and to others called to a great task. Here the presence of God will be more than help from outside: he will take flesh in her.
Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I am a virgin?”

Literally, “since I do not know a man”, as the POC keeps it. Mary does not doubt, as Zechariah did (1:18); she asks how. Her question shows that she does not expect to conceive through Joseph, and the Church has always read it in the light of her virginity.
The angel said to her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God.
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her.

“Here am I” is the answer of Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah when God called them. The verb “let it be” (genoito) expresses a wish, not mere acceptance. Mary does not only allow God's plan; she desires it.
ch: The Church sees in “full of grace” the sign that Mary was prepared by God from the first moment of her life, preserved from all stain of original sin (CCC 490–492). By her “yes”, given in faith and obedience, she became the Mother of God and freely cooperated in the work of salvation (CCC 494; Lumen Gentium 56). St Bernard, preaching on this Gospel, pictures the whole world, Adam and all his children, waiting at Mary's feet for her answer (in substance).
The Council of Ephesus (431) confessed that Mary is Theotokos, Mother of God, because the one she conceived by the Holy Spirit is truly the eternal Son of the Father (CCC 495).

qa: Why was Zechariah punished for his question, but not Mary?
Zechariah asked for proof: “How will I know that this is so?” (1:18). Mary believed and asked how it would happen. Elizabeth later praises exactly this: “blessed is she who believed” (1:45).
Does Genesis 3:15 speak of Mary?

Its first meaning is the long struggle between humanity and evil, and the promise of a descendant who will win. The Church, reading the whole Bible, sees that descendant in Christ and the woman, in its fullest sense, in Mary, the new Eve (CCC 411).
Why do we call Mary “Mother of God” and not only “Mother of Jesus”?
Because Jesus is one person, the eternal Son of God made man. A mother is mother of a person, not of a nature. So Mary is truly Mother of God (CCC 495).
rite: In the West Syriac year, the season before Yeldo is a chain of announcements: to Zechariah, to Mary, the Visitation, the birth of John, the revelation to Joseph. The Malankara Church walks to Christmas by listening to how God spoke to each person who received him. Today the Church honours Mary as Mother of God, as all the Syriac Fathers did, and St Ephrem sang of her as the one in whom the Lord of all made his dwelling. In the Holy Qurbono, when the Holy Spirit is invoked upon the gifts, the Church asks for the same overshadowing that came upon Mary at Nazareth.
study: God's first question is “Where are you?” Where am I hiding from him at this moment?
Galatians 4:6 says the Spirit cries “Abba” in our hearts. How can I let my prayer this week be the prayer of a child, not of a slave?
Mary asks “How can this be?” and still says yes. What is the difference between doubt and a believing question?
Mary's “let it be” is a desire, not only consent. What would it mean for me to desire God's plan, and not just put up with it?

lead: Today's two readings meet in one word: the heart. Paul thanks God for Philemon, whose love has “refreshed the hearts of the saints”, and Jesus teaches that “out of the abundance of the heart” the mouth speaks. A good tree is known by its fruit; Philemon is known by his love. The Church also remembers St Clement of Rome, whose letter to the Corinthians is one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

r.h: The hearts of the saints refreshed
set: Philemon is the shortest of Paul's letters. Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a Christian householder (probably at Colossae), about Onesimus, Philemon's slave, who had run away, met Paul, and become a Christian. Paul is sending him back and asks Philemon to receive him “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (v. 16). Today's verses are the greeting and thanksgiving that prepare that request.
str: vv. 1–3: the greeting: Paul and Timothy, to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in his house.
vv. 4–7: the thanksgiving: Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, and prays that his sharing in the faith may bear fruit.
kw: The common life that comes from faith in Christ. Paul will soon ask Philemon to show that koinōnia toward a runaway slave.
Literally the inner organs, the seat of deep feeling. The word comes back in v. 12 (Onesimus is Paul's “own heart”) and v. 20 (“Refresh my heart in Christ”).
To give rest. Philemon gives rest to the saints; Paul will ask him to give the same rest to Paul's heart by welcoming Onesimus (v. 20).
vv: to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in your house:
A private letter is addressed to a whole church. In the first centuries Christians met in homes. Philemon's decision about Onesimus will be made before the community.
I have indeed received much joy and encouragement from your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, my brother.
Paul praises before he asks. His praise is sincere, and it also reminds Philemon who he already is: a man whose love gives rest to others.
ch: Paul does not write a treatise against slavery, but he places master and slave in the same family, as brothers in the Lord, and so plants the seed that would in time destroy the institution. The Catechism points to this letter when it teaches that enslaving human beings is a sin against their dignity (CCC 2414). The phrase “the church in your house” lies behind the Church's teaching that the Christian family is a “domestic church” (Lumen Gentium 11; CCC 1655–1656).

r.h: A tree is known by its fruit
set: These verses belong to the Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:20–49), Luke's shorter form of the teaching Matthew gives as the Sermon on the Mount. They come after the warning about judging others (6:37–42) and before the parable of the two houses (6:46–49).
str: vv. 43–44: the picture: good and bad trees, figs and thorns.
v. 45: the meaning: the heart is a treasury, and words come out of what is stored there.
kw: Throughout the Bible, the visible result of what a person is. Jesus does not ask us to inspect leaves but fruit.
The heart is a storeroom. What we put into it day by day is what will come out.
Overflow. Speech is the overflow of a full heart.
vv: for each tree is known by its own fruit. Figs are not gathered from thorns, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush.
The images are taken from the hills of Galilee, where thorn bushes grew beside vineyards. You cannot pretend a fruit you do not have.
The good person out of the good treasure of the heart produces good, and the evil person out of evil treasure produces evil; for it is out of the abundance of the heart that the mouth speaks.
Jesus moves from deeds to words. Our speech, especially when we are not careful, shows what we have been storing inside.
ch: The Catechism teaches that sin, like good, has its root in the heart (CCC 1853, citing Matthew 15:19–20). St Augustine, preaching on the good and bad tree, tells his people not to try to change the fruit first, but the tree: change the heart, and the deeds will change (in substance). Conversion is the work of grace in the heart before it is a change of behaviour.

study: Paul says Philemon's love “refreshed” the saints. Who has refreshed my heart this year, and whose heart can I refresh this week?
What have I been storing in the “treasury” of my heart through what I watch, read and think about?

lead: Both readings look toward the coming of Christ. Titus speaks of two appearings: the grace of God “has appeared” in Jesus' first coming, and we wait for “the manifestation of the glory” at his second. Between them is the present age, in which grace trains us to live well. In Matthew, Jesus teaches his disciples to read the signs like a farmer reads a fig tree, and yet to leave the day and the hour to the Father. In the weeks before Yeldo these texts teach us to wait with open eyes and quiet trust.

r.h: The grace of God has appeared
set: The Letter to Titus is one of the three Pastoral Letters. Paul has left Titus in Crete to organise the young churches (1:5). Chapter 2 gives practical advice to older men and women, young people and slaves (2:1–10). Today's verses give the reason behind all that advice: the grace of God that has appeared in Christ. Verses 11–14 are read in many Churches at the Christmas night liturgy.
str: v. 11: grace has appeared, for the salvation of all.
v. 12: grace educates: turn away from what is ungodly, live well “in the present age”.
v. 13: we wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of Christ's glory.
v. 14: who Christ is for us: he gave himself to redeem and purify a people.
v. 15: Titus must teach this with authority.
kw: From the same root as “epiphany”, a word used for the visible arrival of a god or a king. The true epiphany is the coming of God's grace in Jesus.
From paideia, the education of a child. Grace is not only a gift but a teacher, who forms us patiently.
The return of Christ in glory. Christian hope is not a vague wish but a person who will come.
vv: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all,
“To all”: the grace that appeared in Bethlehem is for every human being, not for a few.
while we wait for the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.

A note on the text. In Greek one article governs both titles, “God and Savior”, and most scholars, with the NRSV, take both to refer to Jesus Christ: this is one of the clearest New Testament texts calling Jesus God. The POC translates as two persons, “of our great God and of our Saviour Jesus Christ”. The Greek grammar favours the first reading.
He it is who gave himself for us that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people of his own who are zealous for good deeds.
“A people of his own” echoes Exodus 19:5, where Israel is God's treasured possession. The Church is formed by Christ's self-gift.
ch: The Church reads this passage at Christmas because it holds both comings together: the first, in humility, and the second, in glory. The Roman liturgy echoes verse 13 after the Lord's Prayer, as the Church prays “as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Saviour, Jesus Christ”. Grace is not a reason to relax our effort but the power that makes a holy life possible.

r.h: Learn from the fig tree
set: Jesus is on the Mount of Olives, facing the Temple, speaking of its coming destruction and of the end of the age (Matthew 24:1–3). The disciples asked two questions: when will this be, and what will be the sign of your coming? These verses answer both, in two different ways.
str: vv. 32–33: the parable of the fig tree: the signs can be read.
v. 34: “this generation” will see “all these things”.
v. 35: the words of Jesus will never pass away.
v. 36: the day and hour are known only to the Father.
kw: Most trees in Palestine keep their leaves in winter, but the fig loses them, so its new leaves are a clear sign that summer is near.
The people living at that time. Many commentators refer “all these things” to the events leading to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which that generation did see.
Heaven and earth are the most stable things we know; Jesus' words are more stable still. Only God could say this.
vv: So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
Jesus speaks of his own words as Isaiah spoke of God's word: “the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8).
“But about that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
A note on the text. Some later manuscripts of Matthew leave out “nor the Son”; the oldest include it, and Mark 13:32 has it.
ch: On the words “nor the Son”, the Catechism explains that what Jesus said he did not know, he elsewhere said he was not sent to reveal (CCC 474, citing Mark 13:32 and Acts 1:7). Christ in his human knowledge was united to the divine Person and knew all that he came to reveal. The Church does not set dates for the end: she keeps watch, because the Lord can come at any time (CCC 673).

qa: Did Jesus really not know the day of the end?
The Catechism says that his statement means this was not part of his mission to reveal (CCC 474). The point for us is not to calculate the date but to be ready.
study: Titus 2:12 says grace “trains” us. What is grace teaching me at present, and am I a willing pupil?
What “signs” in my own life tell me the Lord is near, “at the very gates”?

lead: Today's readings are about seeing and proclaiming. Paul, in chains, rejoices that Christ is proclaimed, even by those who preach out of rivalry. Jesus tells his disciples that they are blessed because they see and hear what prophets longed for. The Gospel is a gift to be received with open eyes and handed on with joy, whatever it costs the messenger.

r.h: Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice
set: Paul writes to the church at Philippi, the first church he founded in Europe and the one closest to his heart. He is in prison, most likely in Rome (or possibly Ephesus), waiting for a verdict that could mean death. Some local preachers have become bolder because of his imprisonment, but some are using it to compete with him.
str: vv. 15–17: two kinds of preachers: some from love, others from rivalry.
v. 18: Paul's surprising verdict: Christ is proclaimed, and he rejoices.
vv. 19–20: his hope: by their prayers and the Spirit, all will turn to his salvation; Christ will be exalted in his body, by life or by death.
kw: Originally the self-seeking of someone who works only for pay or for party. Paul uses it again in 2:3: “Do nothing from selfish ambition”.
Paul borrows the words of Job 13:16 in the Greek Old Testament, “this will turn out for my salvation”. Like Job, he trusts that God will vindicate him, whatever the human verdict.
A vivid word: to watch with head stretched forward. Paul uses it also in Romans 8:19 of creation waiting for God's children to be revealed.
vv: What does it matter? Just this, that Christ is proclaimed in every way, whether out of false motives or true; and in that I rejoice.
Paul cares more about Christ being preached than about who gets the credit. He does not approve of rivalry, but he refuses to let it rob him of joy.

It is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be put to shame in any way, but that by my speaking with all boldness, Christ will be exalted now as always in my body, whether by life or by death.
“In my body”: Paul glorifies Christ not only with words but with his whole person, chains included.
ch: The next verse, “For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain” (1:21), is quoted by the Catechism in its teaching on Christian death (CCC 1010). The Church sees in Paul the model of the apostle who rejoices in the Gospel's progress more than in his own success, and who makes even prison a pulpit.

r.h: Blessed are your eyes, for they see
set: Matthew 13 gathers seven parables of the Kingdom. After the parable of the sower (13:1–9), the disciples ask why Jesus speaks to the crowds in parables. His answer, before he explains the sower (13:18–23), quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, the words God gave the prophet at his call.
str: v. 10: the disciples' question.
vv. 11–12: the gift: to know the secrets of the Kingdom; to the one who has, more is given.
vv. 13–15: the reason: they see and do not perceive; Isaiah's prophecy is fulfilled.
vv. 16–17: the blessing on the disciples, who see what prophets longed to see.
kw: Not puzzles but God's plan, once hidden and now revealed in Jesus. It is given, not earned.
Behind it stands the Hebrew māšāl, which covers proverbs, riddles and comparisons. A parable both reveals and hides: it opens itself to those who come closer.
Literally “has grown fat”: a heart thickened and insensitive, no longer able to feel God's word.
vv: He answered, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.
The reason I speak to them in parables is that ‘seeing they do not perceive, and hearing they do not listen, nor do they understand.’

Mark 4:12 says “in order that” they may not see; Matthew says “because” they do not see. Matthew stresses that the hardness comes first, from the hearers, and that parables meet it with mercy, inviting them to look again.
But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.
The disciples are not cleverer than the crowds. They are blessed because they stay near Jesus and ask him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' invitation to the Kingdom comes in parables, which call for a decision: one must give everything, and words are not enough. To those who stay “outside”, everything remains enigmatic (CCC 546). The Church hears verse 16 as a word to every believer who hears the Gospel and receives the sacraments: what kings and prophets longed for is given to us.

qa: Does Jesus speak in parables so that people will not understand?
No. In Matthew the reason is that their hearts are already dull (13:15). Parables are a gentle way to draw the listener to come closer and ask, as the disciples did.
study: Paul rejoices that Christ is preached even by rivals. Where do I need to let go of credit for the good I do?
What have I been given to “see and hear” that the prophets longed for? How can I thank God for it today?

lead: Today's readings show two meals and two powers. Paul tells the Corinthians that they cannot share both the table of the Lord and the table of demons: the cup and the bread unite us with Christ and with one another. In Capernaum Jesus speaks with authority, and an unclean spirit has to leave at his word. The One who drives out evil is the One who gives himself at the table of the Holy Qurbono.

r.h: The cup of blessing and the bread we break
set: Corinth was a city full of temples. Meat sold in the market had often been offered to an idol, and social life included dinners in temple dining rooms. In chapters 8–10 Paul answers questions about this. Here he reaches the heart of the matter: taking part in a sacrificial meal in honour of an idol is incompatible with the Eucharist.
str: vv. 14–15: the command: flee from idolatry; judge for yourselves.
vv. 16–17: the Lord's Supper: the cup and the bread are a sharing in Christ's blood and body, and make us one body.
v. 18: an example from Israel: those who eat the sacrifices share in the altar.
vv. 19–20: idols are nothing, but pagan sacrifice involves demons.
vv. 21–22: the conclusion: you cannot share both tables.
kw: A real participation, not a mere reminder. From this verse the Church calls the reception of the Eucharist “Holy Communion”.
At a Jewish festive meal, the cup over which the thanksgiving was said after the meal; at Passover, one of the four cups. Jesus took such a cup at the Last Supper.
Malachi calls the altar of the Temple “the Lord's table” (Malachi 1:7). Paul uses the same words for the Christian Eucharist.
vv: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?
Paul does not prove the real presence; he takes it for granted as something the Corinthians already believe, and draws a conclusion from it.
Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
The body of Christ we receive makes us the body of Christ we are. Communion with Christ and communion with one another cannot be separated.
You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
ch: The Catechism uses these verses to explain why the Eucharist is called Holy Communion (CCC 1331) and how the Eucharist makes the Church (CCC 1396). St Augustine told the newly baptised: if you are the body of Christ and his members, it is your own mystery that is placed on the Lord's table; be what you see, and receive what you are (in substance, Sermon 272). In the Holy Qurbono the priest breaks the one bread, and the people who share it become one body.

r.h: He commands with authority
set: Jesus has just been rejected at Nazareth (4:16–30). He goes down to Capernaum, a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, which becomes the centre of his ministry. This is the first miracle Luke reports, and it takes place in a synagogue on the Sabbath.
str: vv. 31–32: Jesus teaches, and the people are astounded at his authority.
vv. 33–34: a man with an unclean spirit cries out.
v. 35: Jesus rebukes the spirit, and it leaves without harming the man.
vv. 36–37: amazement, and the report spreads.
kw: The right and the power to act. The scribes taught by quoting earlier teachers; Jesus speaks in his own name.
The demon knows who Jesus is better than the crowd. Knowledge alone is not faith (compare James 2:19).
The same verb is used when Jesus rebukes the fever (4:39) and the wind and waves (8:24). He speaks to evil as its Lord.
vv: They were astounded at his teaching, because he spoke with authority.
“Let us alone! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.”
“What have you to do with us?” is a Semitic way of saying: we have nothing in common. The answer to “Have you come to destroy us?” is yes.
But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” When the demon had thrown him down before them, he came out of him without having done him any harm.
Only Luke adds “without having done him any harm”. Jesus' power over evil is always gentle with the person it frees.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' exorcisms deliver people from the domination of demons and anticipate his great victory over “the ruler of this world”; the coming of God's Kingdom means the defeat of Satan's (CCC 550). The Church continues this ministry in Christ's name, in baptism and, when needed, in exorcism (CCC 1673).

qa: Is Paul saying idols have real power?
No. An idol is nothing (10:19; 8:4). But worship given to what is not God opens a door to evil. Christians must not divide their loyalty.
study: Paul says that “we who are many are one body”. How does my reception of the Holy Qurbono change the way I treat the people beside me?
