Jesus' word releases the man “without having done him any harm”. Where do I need his word to release me today?

lead: Both readings are about faithfulness in ordinary life. Paul tells the Thessalonians to work quietly and not grow weary in doing good. Jesus, asked about divorce, leads his questioners back “to the beginning of creation”, where God made man and woman to become one flesh. Daily work and faithful marriage are two places where the Kingdom is lived, quietly and over many years.

r.h: Do not be weary in doing what is right
set: In Thessalonica some believers had stopped working. The letter does not say exactly why, but chapter 2 shows that some were unsettled by claims that “the day of the Lord is already here” (2:2). Others perhaps simply preferred to live on the generosity of the community. Paul answers with his own example and a firm rule.
str: v. 6: the command: keep away from believers who live in idleness.
vv. 7–9: Paul's example: he worked night and day so as not to be a burden.
v. 10: the rule: anyone unwilling to work should not eat.
vv. 11–12: the problem named, and the remedy: work quietly and earn your own living.
vv. 13–15: do not grow weary in doing good; correct the disobedient as brothers, not enemies.
kw: A military word for a soldier out of rank. The idle are not only lazy; they have stepped out of the ordered life of the community.
A play on words in Greek: not ergazomenous (working) but periergazomenous (working around, meddling). Those who do no work of their own easily busy themselves with others' affairs.
What Paul handed on, by word and example (v. 6; compare 2:15). Christian tradition includes a way of living, not only doctrines.
vv: and we did not eat anyone’s bread without paying for it; but with toil and labor we worked night and day, so that we might not burden any of you.
Paul was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3). He had the right to be supported (v. 9), but he gave it up so that the Gospel would cost his hearers nothing.
For even when we were with you, we gave you this command: Anyone unwilling to work should not eat.
Note the word “unwilling”. The rule is about those who refuse to work, not those who cannot. The Church has always cared for the sick, the old and the unemployed.
Do not regard them as enemies, but warn them as believers.
Even correction is an act of love. The goal is to win back a brother or sister, not to drive them away.
ch: The Catechism quotes 3:10 in its teaching on human work: work is a duty, and through it a person cooperates with the Creator and shares in Christ's redemptive work (CCC 2427). The Didache, an early Christian manual, gives the same rule for a travelling believer who wants to settle in a community: if he has a trade, let him work for his bread; Christ is not to be made a business (in substance, Didache 12).

r.h: What God has joined together
set: Jesus has left Galilee and is on the road to Jerusalem, in Judea and beyond the Jordan, the region ruled by Herod Antipas, who had imprisoned John the Baptist for criticising his marriage (Mark 6:17–18). The question about divorce is a test. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 allowed a husband to give a certificate of dismissal, and the rabbinic schools debated how serious the reason had to be.
str: vv. 1–2: the crowds; the Pharisees' testing question.
vv. 3–5: Jesus' counter-question about Moses, and his explanation: “because of your hardness of heart”.
vv. 6–9: back to the beginning: Genesis 1:27 and 2:24; “what God has joined together, let no one separate”.
vv. 10–12: in the house, the teaching for the disciples: remarriage after divorce is adultery, for both husband and wife.
kw: A word from the Greek Old Testament for a heart closed to God (compare Deuteronomy 10:16). The Law of Moses limited the damage of sin; it did not express God's original plan.
Not only physical union but one life, one shared existence, a new family.
Literally “yoked together”, like two oxen under one yoke. God himself is the one who joins.
vv: But Jesus said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote this commandment for you.
But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’
Jesus answers a legal question by going behind the Law to creation. The question is not “what is permitted?” but “what did God intend?”
Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”
“No one”: not the husband, not the court, not the state. The bond is God's work.
and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.”
Only Mark has this verse. Jewish law did not allow a wife to divorce, but Roman law did, and Mark was writing for Christians who lived under Roman law. Jesus' teaching applies equally to both.
ch: The Church teaches that Jesus restored the original meaning of marriage, and that the permission given by Moses was a concession to hardness of heart (CCC 1614). A valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power (CCC 1640, 2382). At the same time, separation may be permitted in certain cases while the bond remains (CCC 2383), and the Church is called to accompany with care those whose marriages have broken.

qa: Does “anyone unwilling to work should not eat” mean the poor should not be helped?
No. It is about those who refuse to work while able to, and who live off others. Care for the poor, the sick and the unemployed is a constant command of Scripture and of the Church (CCC 2443–2447).
study: Paul says, “Do not be weary in doing what is right.” In which good work am I most tempted to give up?
Jesus takes his hearers back to “the beginning”. How can families in our parish be helped to live God's original plan for marriage?

lead: Today's readings are about small beginnings and patient growth. Paul reminds the Corinthians that he became their father in Christ through the Gospel, and that the Kingdom depends “not on talk but on power”. Jesus compares the Kingdom to a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which becomes a shelter for the birds. The Church honours St Catherine of Alexandria, remembered as a young martyr whose wisdom and courage bore fruit far beyond her short life.

r.h: A father in Christ through the gospel
set: The church at Corinth was divided into groups, each attached to a favourite teacher: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos” (1:12). In chapters 1–4 Paul shows that the preachers are only servants, and that the wisdom of the Cross is not the wisdom of the world. He ends this section with a personal appeal, as a father to his children.
str: v. 15: many guardians, but one father.
vv. 16–17: be imitators of me; Timothy is sent to remind you of my ways.
vv. 18–20: some are arrogant, but Paul will come and test their power, not their talk.
v. 21: the choice: a stick, or love and gentleness.
kw: In a Greek household, the slave who took a child to school and watched over his behaviour. Necessary, but not a parent.
I became your father, I begot you
Paul uses the language of birth. Through his preaching the Corinthians were born into new life in Christ.
Paul does not ask them to copy his personality but his “ways in Christ Jesus” (v. 17). He imitates Christ, and they are to imitate him (11:1).
vv: For though you might have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. Indeed, in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.
“Ten thousand” is a deliberate exaggeration. Teachers can be many; the one through whom you came to faith has a unique bond with you.
For the kingdom of God depends not on talk but on power.
Words alone, however clever, do not make the Kingdom present. The power of God shows itself in changed lives.
What would you prefer? Am I to come to you with a stick, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
A father can correct firmly, but he would rather come in gentleness. The choice is left to the children.
ch: The Church has always seen in this verse the root of spiritual fatherhood: bishops and priests are fathers because they give life in Christ through the word and the sacraments. This is why Christians in Kerala call their priest “Achen”, father. Such fatherhood is a service and a share in the fatherhood of God, “from whom every family in heaven and on earth takes its name” (Ephesians 3:15).

r.h: The mustard seed
set: Mark 4 gathers the parables of seeds: the sower (4:1–20), the seed growing secretly (4:26–29) and the mustard seed. They speak to disciples who may be discouraged: Jesus' ministry seems small, and many reject it. The parables promise that what God has sown will grow.
str: v. 30: a double question: to what shall we compare the Kingdom?
vv. 31–32: the mustard seed: smallest when sown, greatest when grown, a shelter for birds.
vv. 33–34: a summary: Jesus spoke in parables “as they were able to hear”, and explained everything privately to the disciples.
kw: In Jewish speech the mustard seed was proverbial for the smallest thing. The mustard plant of Galilee can grow to two or three metres in a season.
Literally “pitch their tents”. The image of birds nesting in a great tree comes from the prophets (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12), where it pictures a kingdom that shelters the nations.
The disciples receive more because they stay with Jesus. The same pattern is in Mark 4:10.
vv: It is like a mustard seed, which, when sown upon the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth;
yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes the greatest of all shrubs, and puts forth large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.”
Ezekiel's great tree is a noble cedar (Ezekiel 17:23); Jesus chooses a garden shrub. The Kingdom grows great, but it never loses its humble beginning.
With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it;
Jesus adapts his teaching to his hearers' capacity. Good catechesis does the same.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is on earth the seed and the beginning of the Kingdom (Lumen Gentium 5; CCC 764). The parable gives hope to small communities and to every humble beginning made in faith. St Catherine of Alexandria, a young woman of the fourth century, is a fitting example: tradition remembers her as a wise defender of the faith whose witness grew into one of the most loved cults of East and West.

qa: Jesus said, “call no one your father on earth” (Matthew 23:9). Why do we call priests “father”?

Jesus forbids putting anyone in God's place, or seeking titles for pride. He does not forbid the word itself: Paul calls himself the Corinthians' father in Christ (4:15). Spiritual fathers are true fathers only when they lead people to the one Father in heaven.
study: Who has been a “father” or “mother” in Christ to me? How can I thank God for them today?
What small seed of faith or service could I plant this week, trusting God to make it grow?

lead: On the Sunday of the Visitation of Mary, Mother of God, to Elizabeth, the Suboro season moves from Nazareth to the hill country of Judea. The evening Gospel already tells of the meeting (Luke 1:39–45). The Old Testament lessons gather women through whom God worked: Rebekah at the well, who runs to serve a stranger and is chosen to carry the promise (Genesis 24:15–27); Hannah, who sings when God gives her a son (1 Samuel 2:1–11); the capable woman whose “strength and dignity are her clothing” (Proverbs 31:25); and Isaiah's promise that the deaf will hear and “the meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord” (Isaiah 29:19). The Catholic Epistle calls the Church “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9).

The three readings studied here form one song. Hannah sings of the God who lifts up the poor; Paul proclaims the God who “desires everyone to be saved” through one mediator; Mary, carrying that mediator in her womb, sings Hannah's song again in a new key. Visit, joy and praise are the key words of this Sunday.

r.h: Hannah's song
set: Hannah was one of the two wives of Elkanah, and she had no children. Year after year at the shrine of Shiloh she wept, and she prayed so intensely that the priest Eli thought she was drunk (1 Samuel 1:12–14). God heard her, and she bore Samuel. When the child was weaned she brought him to Shiloh and gave him to the Lord. Her song is her response.

Many scholars think the song was an older hymn of Israel, placed on Hannah's lips because it fits her story. It ends with a king and an “anointed one” (v. 10), though Israel had no king yet; it looks forward to David, and beyond him to the Messiah.
str: v. 1: Hannah's joy: “My heart exults in the Lord”.
vv. 2–3: there is no Holy One like the Lord; a warning to the proud.
vv. 4–8: the great reversals: the mighty broken, the feeble strengthened; the barren bears seven; the poor raised from the dust.
vv. 9–10: the Lord guards his faithful, judges the earth and strengthens his anointed.
v. 11: Elkanah goes home; the boy Samuel stays to serve the Lord.
kw: In v. 1, “my strength is exalted” is literally “my horn is lifted up”, an image from a wild ox raising its horns. The same word returns in v. 10, “the power of his anointed”. Zechariah's song uses it for Christ, the “horn of salvation” (Luke 1:69, NRSV “a mighty savior”).
A title of God in the Psalms and Deuteronomy: firm, safe, unchanging. The POC renders it “a sure refuge”.
The first time in the Bible that a king is called God's anointed. In Greek this is christos. Hannah's song, at the beginning of the books of Samuel, already points to the Messiah.
vv: Hannah prayed and said, “My heart exults in the Lord; my strength is exalted in my God.
Hannah's prayer begins with joy in God himself, not first in the gift. Mary will begin the same way: “my spirit rejoices in God my Savior”.
He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor.
The ash heap outside a town was where beggars and lepers sat. God's way is to turn the world's order upside down. Psalm 113:7–8 repeats these words almost exactly.
The Lord will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king, and exalt the power of his anointed.
ch: The Catechism names Hannah, the mother of Samuel, among the holy women of the Old Covenant whose mission prepared for that of Mary (CCC 489). The Fathers and all later commentators have noticed how closely Mary's Magnificat follows Hannah's song: the joy in God, the lowly lifted up, the hungry filled, the proud brought down. In Hannah, a barren woman who gives her only son to God, the Church sees a figure of Mary who offers her Son, and of the Church who rejoices in the God who lifts up the poor.

r.h: God desires everyone to be saved
set: In the First Letter to Timothy, Paul instructs his co-worker, who leads the church at Ephesus, on the order of community life. Chapter 2 begins with a call to pray “for everyone, for kings and all who are in high positions” (2:1–2). Today's verses give the reason: the God to whom we pray wants all to be saved. Then Paul speaks of how men and women should pray and present themselves in the assembly.
str: v. 4: God's will: everyone saved, everyone knowing the truth.
vv. 5–6: a short creed: one God, one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.
v. 7: Paul appointed herald, apostle and teacher of the Gentiles.
v. 8: men are to pray with holy hands lifted up, without anger.
vv. 9–10: women are to adorn themselves with modesty and good works, not with costly display.
kw: One who stands between two parties to reconcile them. Christ can be the one mediator because he is both God and “himself human”.
The only place this form is found in the New Testament. It echoes Jesus' own words: the Son of Man came “to give his life a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Here Paul says “for all”.
Related to kosmos (order, ornament). True adornment is an ordered life, shown in good works.
vv: who desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
This verse is the reason for praying for everyone, even rulers who persecute. No one lies outside God's saving desire.
For there is one God; there is also one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human,
“One God” is the faith of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4). “One mediator” is the faith of the Church. Christ's mediation does not compete with anyone; it makes room for others to share in it.
I desire, then, that in every place the men should pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or argument;
Standing with lifted hands was the common posture of prayer for Jews and early Christians. Prayer and quarrelling do not go together.
but with good works, as is proper for women who profess reverence for God.
The point of vv. 9–10 is not a dress code but where beauty is found. Mary, the handmaid of the Lord, is the model of a woman adorned with faith and service.
ch: The Catechism quotes 2:4 to show that God wants all to be saved and to know the truth, which is why the Church is missionary (CCC 74, 851). On the one mediator, the Second Vatican Council teaches that Mary's maternal role “in no way obscures or diminishes this unique mediation of Christ, but rather shows its power”; it flows from Christ's merits and depends entirely on him (Lumen Gentium 60; CCC 970). Mary at the Visitation is the clearest picture of this: she brings Christ to Elizabeth, and all the joy comes from him.

r.h: The Visitation and the Magnificat
set: Right after the Annunciation, Mary goes to visit Elizabeth, whose pregnancy the angel had given her as a sign (1:36). Luke does not name the town; an ancient tradition places it at Ein Karem, a few kilometres west of Jerusalem. From Nazareth that is a journey of several days.

Luke tells the story with echoes of 2 Samuel 6, when King David brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. David asked, “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (2 Samuel 6:9); Elizabeth asks, “why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?” David danced before the ark; John leaps in the womb. The ark stayed in the house of Obed-edom three months (2 Samuel 6:11); Mary stays with Elizabeth about three months. Many Fathers and Catholic commentators see Mary as the new ark, carrying God's presence.
str: vv. 39–40: the journey and the greeting.
vv. 41–45: Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, blesses Mary and her child and praises her faith.
vv. 46–50: the Magnificat, first part: what God has done for Mary.
vv. 51–55: second part: what God does for his people: reversals, mercy, the promise to Abraham.
v. 56: Mary stays about three months and returns home.
kw: Not nervous hurry but eager readiness. The Greek word also carries the sense of zeal. Love does not delay.

The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for Jacob and Esau struggling in Rebekah's womb (Genesis 25:22). Here the child leaps not in struggle but “for joy” (v. 44). John begins his mission as forerunner before he is born.
To make great, to declare great. Mary cannot make God greater; she makes his greatness known. The Latin first word, Magnificat, gives the song its name.
Humble condition, low estate. God looks on what the world overlooks, as he looked on Hannah's misery (1 Samuel 1:11).
vv: When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the child leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit
Mary speaks, and the Spirit comes. Where Mary brings Christ, the Holy Spirit fills hearts with joy.
And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?
“My Lord” is the title the Old Testament gives to God and to the Messiah king (Psalm 110:1). Elizabeth is the first to call Mary, in effect, Mother of God.
And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.”
Mary's first blessedness is her faith. Jesus himself will say the same: blessed are those who hear the word of God and obey it (11:28).
for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed;
A prophecy fulfilled every time the Church sings to Mary or prays the Hail Mary.
ch: The Catechism notes that John was “filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb” and that the Visitation was a visit of God to his people (CCC 717). Elizabeth's greeting forms the first part of the Hail Mary (CCC 2676). The Magnificat is “the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church” (CCC 2619), and the words “all generations will call me blessed” are the foundation of the Church's devotion to Mary (CCC 971).

St Ambrose, commenting on this Gospel, wished that the soul of Mary might be in each believer to magnify the Lord, and her spirit in each to rejoice in God (in substance). The Magnificat is not only Mary's song but the song of every lowly person whom God has visited.

qa: If Christ is the “one mediator”, why do we ask Mary to pray for us?

Because her prayer, like the prayers we ask of one another, depends entirely on Christ and leads to him. The Church teaches that Mary's role shows the power of Christ's mediation rather than diminishing it (Lumen Gentium 60; CCC 970). At the Visitation she brings Christ, and Elizabeth is filled with the Spirit.
Did Mary herself compose the Magnificat?

Luke presents it as Mary's song, and the Church prays it as hers. It is woven from the Psalms and Hannah's song, the prayers a devout young woman of Israel would know by heart. Mary prays the Scriptures and makes them her own.
Why does the Magnificat speak of the mighty brought down? Is it a political song?

It speaks of God's way of acting in history, which overturns pride and lifts up the lowly. It is not a call to hatred but a warning to the proud and a hope for the poor, and it calls the Church to share God's care for the poor (CCC 2448).
rite: The Malankara faithful have a deep love for St Mary, the Mother of God, shown in many prayers and in the fast of the first eight days of September before the feast of her birth. On this Sunday the Church sees in Mary the model of the one who receives Christ and at once goes out to serve. In the Holy Qurbono we receive the same Lord whom Mary carried to Elizabeth; the Visitation teaches us to carry him from the altar into the homes of the sick, the elderly and the lonely. As the Suboro season moves toward Yeldo, many Malankara families prepare by prayer and fasting, so that their hearts, like Elizabeth's house, may be ready to welcome him.
study: Hannah and Mary both begin with joy in God himself, not first in his gifts. What would it mean for my prayer to begin there?
1 Timothy 2:4 says God desires everyone to be saved. For whom, outside my circle, should I pray this week?
Mary went “with haste” to serve. Who is the Elizabeth near me, waiting for a visit?
Which line of the Magnificat do I most need to make my own this Advent journey to Yeldo?

lead: On the feast of Mar Andrews Shleeha, St Andrew the Apostle, the readings speak of how Christ is first found and then formed in us. In John's Gospel Andrew hears the Baptist's word, follows Jesus, stays with him, and at once brings his brother Simon. In Galatians Paul, like a mother in labour, longs for Christ to be “formed” in his converts. Finding Christ is the beginning; letting him take shape in us, and bringing others to him, is the whole Christian life.

r.h: Until Christ is formed in you
set: After a long argument from Scripture (Galatians 3:1–4:11), Paul changes his tone. He turns from argument to a personal appeal, reminding the Galatians of their first meeting and of the love they once showed him. Teachers who demanded circumcision had won their hearts, and Paul fears he has lost his children.
str: v. 12: “become as I am, for I also have become as you are”.
vv. 13–15: memories: Paul came to them ill, and they received him like an angel of God, like Christ himself.
vv. 16–18: has telling the truth made him their enemy? The rivals court them for the wrong reasons.
vv. 19–20: the image of childbirth, and Paul's wish to be with them.
kw: Paul does not say what the illness was. Some suggest an eye disease because of v. 15, but this is only a guess. What matters is that God used his weakness to bring the Gospel.
to be in the pain of childbirth
A strong image. Paul is not only a father (1 Corinthians 4:15) but a mother, suffering the labour pains of bringing them to life in Christ, now a second time.
The word is used of an embryo taking shape. The goal of the Christian life is not only to believe in Christ but to have his own form, his likeness, grow within us.
vv: Friends, I beg you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You have done me no wrong.
Paul, a Jew, became like a Gentile, living without the Law's ceremonies among them. Now he asks them to become like him: children of God in Christ, not slaves again.
though my condition put you to the test, you did not scorn or despise me, but welcomed me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

In the ancient world sickness could be seen as a curse, and the Greek of v. 14 literally says “you did not spit”, a gesture against evil. The Galatians saw Christ in a sick stranger, as Jesus taught (Matthew 25:40).
My little children, for whom I am again in the pain of childbirth until Christ is formed in you,
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church, contemplating Mary, “becomes herself a mother”: by preaching and baptism she brings to new and immortal life children conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of God (Lumen Gentium 64). Paul's labour pains are the Church's own: every pastor, catechist and parent shares in this work of forming Christ in others. Coming at the start of the journey to Yeldo, the verse reminds us that Christ who was formed in Mary's womb wants to be formed in each of us.

r.h: Come and see
set: John's Gospel opens with a sequence of days (1:29, 35, 43; 2:1). John the Baptist has already pointed Jesus out as “the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world” (1:29). Today's passage is the day after: two of the Baptist's disciples leave their master to follow Jesus, and one of them is Andrew. The first disciples come to Jesus through the witness of another.
Andrew, a fisherman from Bethsaida (1:44), was the brother of Simon Peter. The other disciple is not named; many think it is the Beloved Disciple himself, who never names himself in this Gospel.
str: vv. 35–36: the Baptist sees Jesus and says, “Look, here is the Lamb of God!”
v. 37: two disciples hear and follow Jesus.
vv. 38–39: Jesus' first words: “What are you looking for?” “Come and see.” They stay with him.
vv. 40–41: Andrew finds his brother: “We have found the Messiah.”
v. 42: Andrew brings Simon to Jesus, who gives him a new name, Cephas.
kw: It gathers several Old Testament images: the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the servant led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7), and the lamb God himself will provide (Genesis 22:8).
to stay, to remain, to abide
A key word in John. The disciples ask where Jesus “stays” and they “remained” with him. Later Jesus will say, “Abide in me as I abide in you” (15:4). Discipleship is staying with Jesus.
The Aramaic kêpā means rock; in Greek it is Petros. A new name in the Bible means a new mission, as with Abram and Jacob.
The Hebrew and Aramaic word for “anointed”, which the evangelist translates into Greek as Christos.
vv: When Jesus turned and saw them following, he said to them, “What are you looking for?” They said to him, “Rabbi” (which translated means Teacher), “where are you staying?”
The first words of Jesus in John's Gospel are a question about desire. He does not begin with a command but asks what we are seeking.
He said to them, “Come and see.” They came and saw where he was staying, and they remained with him that day. It was about four o’clock in the afternoon.
Literally “the tenth hour”, as the POC keeps it. The detail sounds like the memory of an eyewitness who never forgot the hour his life changed.
He first found his brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which is translated Anointed).
Andrew's first act as a disciple is to bring someone else. He found Christ, and at once he wanted his brother to find him too.
He brought Simon to Jesus, who looked at him and said, “You are Simon son of John. You are to be called Cephas” (which is translated Peter).
ch: The Eastern Churches call Andrew the Prōtoklētos, the “First-called”, because he was among the first to follow Jesus. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this Gospel, praises Andrew because, once he had learned from Jesus, he did not keep the treasure to himself but ran to share it with his brother (in substance). Every Christian vocation follows this pattern: someone points to Christ, we come and stay with him, and then we bring others.
Tradition says that Andrew preached in Greece and the lands around the Black Sea and was martyred at Patras on a cross; the X-shaped cross associated with him comes from later tradition.

qa: Why does Jesus change Simon's name before Simon has done anything?
Because the name is God's gift and mission, not a reward. Jesus sees what Simon will become by grace. Andrew brings him, but Jesus calls him.
What does “Lamb of God” mean?

It joins the Passover lamb whose blood saved Israel, the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 and the lamb God provides in Genesis 22. Jesus is the one sacrifice that takes away the sin of the world (CCC 608).
rite: Andrew and Peter were brothers, and the Church sees their brotherhood in the Churches that honour them. Peter is remembered in Antioch, the mother Church of the West Syriac tradition to which the Malankara Church belongs, and in Rome, while Constantinople honours Andrew as its patron. Every year on this feast the Pope sends a delegation to the Ecumenical Patriarch, and the Patriarch sends one to Rome for Sts Peter and Paul: a sign of the longing for full unity among Christians. On Mar Andrews' feast the Malankara faithful pray for that unity and ask for Andrew's zeal to bring their own brothers and sisters to Christ.
study: Jesus asks, “What are you looking for?” How would I answer him honestly today?
Andrew first found his own brother. Who in my family or neighbourhood could I bring closer to Christ?
Paul longs for Christ to be “formed” in his people. What part of Christ's likeness is still taking shape in me?
